title: Routes Down and Right
statement:
A robot stands in the top-left cell of a grid with m rows and n columns. It wants to reach the bottom-right cell. Each move takes it one cell right or one cell down, never left or up.

Return how many different routes lead from the start to the goal. Two routes are different if they visit a different sequence of cells.

examples.why: Every route is 2 downs and 3 rights in some order. Choosing where the 2 downs go among 5 moves gives 10.
A single row: the only route is straight right. The answer is 1, not 0, even though there is no choice to make.
Not 2 × 2 per cell or m × n: routes share their first cells, so count them by how they arrive, not by multiplying choices.

hints: Look at the goal cell. The robot's last move into it came either from the cell above or from the cell to the left. Nothing else is possible.
So the number of routes into any cell is the routes into the cell above plus the routes into the cell to its left. What are the counts along the top row and the left column?

Fill a table row by row, left to right: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1], with 1 everywhere in row 0 and column 0. Each row only needs the row above, so one array that you update in place is enough.

explain.intuition:
This is the problem to learn 2-D dynamic programming on. Four questions set up every table in this section.

1. What does one cell of the table mean? Let dp[i][j] be the number of routes from the start to cell (i, j). The answer is dp[m−1][n−1]. 2. Which cells does it depend on? Think about the last move into (i, j): it came from above, (i−1, j), or from the left, (i, j−1). Those two sets of routes never overlap, because their last step differs, and together they cover every route. So dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. 3. Where does it start? Cells in row 0 or column 0 can be reached only by a straight line, so they hold 1. 4. In what order do you fill it? Any order in which the cell above and the cell to the left are already done: row by row, left to right, like reading a page.

Then look at what the fill order actually reads. Row i only uses row i−1 and the part of row i already written. So keep one row. Before you update row[j] it still holds the value from the row above, and row[j−1] already holds the new value to the left. row[j] += row[j−1] does the whole recurrence. This "cut to one row" trick comes back in almost every problem in this section.
steps: Make row of length n, filled with 1. That is row 0: one straight route to each cell.
Repeat m − 1 times, once per remaining row. Column 0 stays 1.
For j from 1 to n − 1: row[j] = row[j] + row[j − 1]. The old row[j] is "from above"; row[j − 1] is "from the left", already updated for this row.
pitfalls: Starting the edges at 0. A single row or column still has exactly one route, as in the second example.
Filling right to left in the one-row version. Then row[j − 1] still holds the previous row's value and the counts come out wrong.
Plain recursion without remembering results. The same cell is reached by many routes, so the call tree grows like the answer itself, into the billions.

solutions.title: Recursion on the last move
solutions.idea: Routes into a cell are routes into the cell above plus routes into the cell to the left. Recurse without remembering anything, so shared cells are recounted over and over.

solutions.title: Full table
solutions.idea: Fill dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1] row by row, with 1 along the top row and the left column.

solutions.title: One row, updated in place
solutions.idea: Each row only reads the row above. Before row[j] is updated it still holds 'from above', and row[j − 1] already holds 'from the left'.

followups: Every route is m − 1 downs and n − 1 rights in some order. Can you get the answer from a single binomial coefficient, and how do you compute it without overflow?
Some cells are blocked. What changes in the table?
Each cell has a cost and you want the cheapest route instead of the count. Which part of the recurrence changes?
